book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake

chapters.relation: Editor Kristopher Phillips's introduction explains why the Bluths deserve a philosophy book: Buster embodies the academic fear of the perpetual graduate student whose esoteric scholarship (cartography, seventeenth-century agrarian economics) prepares him for nothing, while Tobias is the over-credentialed scholar with no common sense at all, as the 'analrapist' business cards show. The introduction promises that seventeenth-century philosophy and older ideas illuminate everyday life in the O.C. (don't call it that) and might keep readers from emulating Gob's huge mistakes.

Tests Socrates' claim (via Plato's Apology and the Myth of the Cave) that the self-examined life is the happiest against the Bluths: Michael, the one who escapes the cave in the pilot (learning at the boat party that his father is a criminal and he was never getting partnership), turns out chronically miserable, while self-deceivers Gob, Lindsay, and Tobias are mostly content. The chapter concludes that Bertrand Russell's Conquest of Happiness fits better: reflection makes sinners (George Michael's self-loathing over Maeby), narcissists (Michael's need to be seen as good), and megalomaniacs (Kitty) unhappy, so the unexamined life is not a huge mistake, though moderate examination still pays.

Asks what, if anything, makes George Michael kissing Maeby wrong, and dismantles the Argument from Naturalism by testing three definitions of 'natural' against incest, Gob's Segway, and Buster's devotion to Lucille (and Maeby possibly being 'made in a cup' via IVF), showing the argument equivocates in violation of Hume's is/ought distinction. It then weighs Ayer's emotivism (moral claims as 'Yuck!' expressions) against Leon Kass's wisdom of repugnance, concluding the disgust at cousin-kissing may be an aesthetic rather than a moral judgment.

Runs the Bluths through Freudian psychoanalysis: George Sr. hiding in the attic ('Sad Sack', 'Good Grief!') illustrates the unconscious, preconscious, and repression; Michael acts as ego mediating the family's id demands (the unfrozen stock spree) against George Michael's super-ego; Tobias dressing as a pirate among homosexuals and Michael's 'brother...bother' and 'Egg' slips are parapraxes betraying repressed desire; Buster's Motherboy dates and 'Why I Want to Marry My Mother' enact a failed Oedipus complex; and the brothers' scheme against George Sr. in 'Making a Stand' reenacts the primal horde of Totem and Taboo, origin of the incest taboo that haunts George Michael and Maeby.

Uses Sartre's cafe waiter, directly mirrored when Gob play-acts a waiter in 'S.O.B.s', to define bad faith as denying one's freedom by disappearing into roles: illusionist, Bluth Company president in George Sr.'s suit, 'any man' winning back Marta, Ward Cleaver father to Steve Holt (!). Distinguishing bad faith from impossible self-deception (beings-for-themselves have no pre-given essence), the chapter argues that even sincerity ('be yourself, Gob') is bad faith, and provocatively concludes Gob is happier and kinder to others in bad faith, reversing Socrates' 'know thyself'.

Applies Marx's fourfold alienation (from product, from labor, from species-being, from others) to Bluth capitalism: George Michael dips and sells bananas he cannot keep, Lupe cleans Lucille's home under duress, and classes divide the family from the people it exploits. George Sr.'s Boyfights tapes and Caged Wisdom show the capitalist commodifying his children and himself, Gob's figurehead presidency turns employees into resources, Lindsay is 'having without being', and Engels's property-based account of the nuclear family explains Tobias's repressed sexuality; the cure offered is democratic socialism, since within-system fixes only get more absurd.

Audits the Bluth Company's 'Family First' creed against theories of corporate social responsibility, the shareholder-profit model it actually follows versus the stakeholder model of Johnson & Johnson's credo. Evidence includes the Cornballer that burns everyone yet sells in Mexico, the sinking model home and the two-week fake house built 'not good, just looking good', child labor at the banana stand, Boyfights, unpaid construction crews, and the Iraq homes built for Saddam as a CIA wiretapping scheme. The chapter concludes that Family First only arrests the company's moral development, a manual for how not to run a business.

Reads Bluth bourgeois identity through Marx's class vocabulary: consumption as status display (Lucille's furs, $6,300 suits), labor-as-leisure (Tobias's acting, Buster's cartography, Gob's illusions), and the observation that the family's real workers are children, women of color like Lupe, and a Roomba. Class is performed, as Tom Jane's homeless method acting and Lucille's 'poolside only' meltdown show, and the Bluths' narcissism (Lindsay's cause-shopping activism, the family's disgust at Buster's severed hand) is analyzed as a form of bourgeois privilege, while the family fails at the reinvestment that would make it a proper bourgeoisie.

Argues, with Aristotle's social animal and Hegel's recognition (via Charles Taylor), that identity is dialogical and needs others' confirmation, which explains Gob's misery as an unrecognized illusionist and Buster as an unrespected scholar. But 'imperial' identities like race get forced on people: Buster's 'slave buddies' fantasy of Mexico, Lucille's 'room full of waiters', Michael failing to recognize Lupe, and Gob's puppet Franklin, whose bleaching and 'George Bush doesn't care about black puppets' spoof the false essentialism Appiah calls racialism. The chapter's ethics of identity urges treating identities as recreational rather than essential.

Treats the show's wordplay as a working laboratory for philosophy of language: Gob's brother-in-law confusion in 'Whistler's Mother' separates speaker meaning from sentence meaning, George Michael and Maeby's accidental wedding before a real priest in 'Fakin' It' and Lucille's weaponized 'I've been a horrible mother' illustrate J. L. Austin's performative speech acts (doing things with words), and Tobias's 'I just blue myself', the 'fire... sale' audition, and the literal doctor's 'he's going to be all right' turn on H. P. Grice's conversational implicature and the cooperative principle, showing that meaning is never graspable outside context and that the hearer's role is active.

Uses the sex/gender distinction drawn since Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex to read Tobias: biologically male but performing femininity (knitting, Mrs. Featherbottom, crying in the shower in cutoffs), he exposes our false conflations of sex, gender, and sexual orientation behind the running 'Tobias is gay' gag. His interchangeable pronoun use (Steve Holt (!) is a 'she' when cast as Beatrice) and 'buy-curious' double entendres embody the claim that gender is something we do rather than are, and the chapter proposes him as an androgynous, possibly pansexual ideal whose real 'problem' is society's gender biases, not his.

Sorts the Oscar/George Sr. twin confusion into the metaphysical, persistence, and evidential problems of personal identity, testing Aristotle's essential properties (why two actresses play one Marta, what makes each Richter brother distinct) and Descartes's immaterial soul (undermined by surrogate Larry, who stays Larry while Buster remotely operates him). Locke's memory criterion then explains why Oscar is not guilty of George's crimes and why Gob disowns what his forget-me-nows erased, before Thomas Reid's transitivity objection, staged through a lifetime of Gob's roofies, shows Locke committed to old Gob both being and not being young Gob.

Explains Gob's professional failure through Aristotle's account of practices realizing their aims: Gob understands that illusions should surprise and delight, and he is motivated, but he lacks the craft-virtues of the modern illusionist as methodical engineer of experience, namely doggedness, diligence, technical knowhow, and above all humility. Instead he exhibits hubris, the excess opposite the mean, believing magic lives 'in here' in his heart; the 'Sword of Destiny' fiasco (a real sword, Buster's fake hand, a botched surgery) and the yacht that merely sinks show his failure is of character, compounded by the Dunning-Kruger effect that leaves him opaque to himself.

Builds the justified-true-belief account of knowledge from Bluth cases (Tobias's belief in his own acting lacks justification, Michael's belief that he crashed the car under Lucille's manipulation lacks truth), then shows the writers smuggling Gettier cases into the show: George Sr. 'knows for a fact' the government has no case via Cindi Lightballoon's blind faith, Buster forms the true belief that Oscar is his father from George Sr. disguised as Oscar, and Michael's disbelief of Maggie Lizer is luckily true despite the swapped pregnancy bodysuit. The chapter closes by surveying fixes: demanding certainty, Russell's no-false-premises condition, and Goldman-style causal theories of knowing.

Reads the 'Sad Sack' photograph, which Wayne Jarvis sees as Iraqi WMD bunkers and Barry Zuckerkorn sees as Tobias's testicles, through the Duhem-Quine thesis of underdetermination and Kuhn's theory-ladenness of observation: the dominant 'George Sr. the traitor' paradigm dictates what is seen and nearly mobilizes Buster for war, while Barry's rival theory creates a crisis that only the omniscient narrator resolves. Kuhn's five criteria for theory choice (accuracy, consistency, scope, simplicity, fruitfulness) are applied to the rival 'theories', and George Michael's failed eye exam dramatizes the skeptical moment when no lens lets you see clearly, showing knowledge is a social and political position.

Reconstructs the constitutional definition of treason into 'passive-aggressive treason' (enemy, adherence, aid and comfort) and argues George Sr.'s Iraqi mini-palaces for Saddam satisfy all three elements only lightly, given his profit motive and the shoddy construction. The real question is why treason is wrong at all, answered by contrasting instrumental theories of political obligation, under which the Bluths' banana-stand tax fraud harms the state more, with relational theories that ground duties in shared civic bonds like a family, which better capture the communal betrayal of siding with an enemy.

Interrogates Gob's catchphrase 'I've made a huge mistake': on Aristotle's account of hexis, the mean of truthfulness and proper pride, and justice as proportional distribution, Gob's prison-escape key stunt and 'Hermano' jealousy make him wicked rather than merely error-prone, since he lacks grasp of his own injustices. Hume's sentimentalist reply is that immorality is a nonrational moral sense refined only through experience, so mistakes could educate Gob, except he roofies away his one growth moment with Steve Holt (!). MacIntyre's practices (the Magician's Alliance versus non-practitioner Gob) and the narrative unity of character explain why a man who tells no coherent story of himself ends up with no wisdom.

Reads Bluth contradiction through Kant's categorical imperative: Lindsay's lie about her shopgirl job, Gob's jealousy bred by comparative parenting, and George Michael's conformist drift show both the imperative's force and the danger of its empty formalism, while the 'Afternoon Delight' double entendres test whether good intentions suffice for Kantian worth. Nietzsche then answers that morality itself is the contradiction: virtue manufactured from ressentiment ('weakness is being lied into something meritorious'), the will to power turned inward as nihilism, with self-overcoming and value creation as the exit; Mary Douglas's joke theory closes the chapter by explaining why all this contradiction is comic and why the joke is on Gob.

Uses the show's narrator and structure (the chain of contingencies costing Buster his hand, 'now that's how you narrate a story') to argue that we impose narrative on life to make it meaningful, starting from Aristotle's Poetics requirement of beginning, middle, and end. George Sr.'s endlessly reinterpreted J. Walter Weatherman lessons show storytelling as moral choice among possible versions of events, Nietzsche's advice to learn from artists commends styling one's own life aesthetically, and Kierkegaard's 'life must be understood backwards but lived forwards' explains both self-narration and the show's rewatchable 'call forwards', ending on narrative as the sense-making abstraction by which we know ourselves.

holes.name: Emotivism (boo/hurrah theory)
holes.what: A. J. Ayer's view that moral claims merely express emotional approval or disgust rather than state facts that could be proven.
holes.why: Chapter 10 uses emotivism to read 'incest is wrong' as a 'Yuck!' before weighing it against Kass.

holes.name: The Wisdom of Repugnance (the yuck factor)
holes.what: Leon Kass's claim that visceral disgust is the emotional expression of deep moral wisdom that reason cannot fully articulate.
holes.why: Chapter 10's verdict on George Michael and Maeby turns on whether the yuck factor carries moral information.

holes.name: The Oedipus Complex
holes.what: Freud's account of the boy's repressed desire for his mother and rivalry with the prohibitive father, extended in Totem and Taboo to the origin of the incest taboo.
holes.why: Chapter 11 diagnoses Buster's Motherboy devotion and Lucille Two romance as failed repression and reads the brothers' plots against George Sr. as the primal horde.

holes.name: Shareholder vs Stakeholder Theories of Corporate Responsibility
holes.what: The business-ethics debate over whether a corporation's only duty is maximizing shareholder profit or whether it also owes duties to employees, customers, and communities.
holes.why: Chapter 15 measures the Bluth Company's 'Family First' practices against the shareholder model and Johnson & Johnson's stakeholder credo.

holes.name: Speech Acts (performatives)
holes.what: J. L. Austin's theory that utterances like 'I do' or 'I apologize' perform actions rather than describe the world, succeeding only in the right context with the right speaker.
holes.why: Chapter 19 analyzes George Michael and Maeby's accidental wedding and Lucille's guilt-inducing 'I've been a horrible mother' as performatives.

holes.name: Conversational Implicature (Grice's cooperative principle)
holes.what: H. P. Grice's account of how speakers communicate more than they literally say via the cooperative principle and the maxims of quantity, quality, manner, and relation.
holes.why: Chapter 19 explains Tobias's 'I just blue myself' double entendres and the 'fire... sale' audition through implicature rather than explicit meaning.

holes.name: Political Obligation (why obey the state?)
holes.what: The question of what special duty citizens have to obey and support their state, answered by instrumental (public goods) or relational (shared bonds) theories.
holes.why: Chapter 27 needs political obligation to explain why George Sr.'s light treason is blameworthy beyond mere illegality.

holes.name: Douglas's Theory of Jokes
holes.what: Mary Douglas's account of the joke as a symbolic pattern that momentarily deconstructs social hierarchy and gives the mind's monitoring system a holiday (building on Freud).
holes.why: Chapter 29's final section invokes Douglas to explain why the Bluths' contradictions are comic and why the joke is on Gob.

holes.name: Narrative Identity
holes.what: The view associated with Ricoeur and MacIntyre that a self constitutes itself by telling a unified, evolving story of its life.
holes.why: Chapter 31 uses the show's narrator to argue we give ourselves identity and meaning through the stories we tell about ourselves.
